paras: The Findlay Italian strikers' attempted hanging of a paymaster took place on the evening of August 1, 1888, when about 200 Italian laborers on the Mahoning railroad near Findlay, Ohio, procured a rope to hang the paymaster during a dispute over their pay. A sheriff's posse arrived in time to rescue him, and no one was reported hurt. Papers across the country carried the story, some as an Italian strike and others as a threatened "race riot" between Italian and American laborers.

In early July 1888, several hundred Italian laborers were at work in and around Findlay, 400 or 500 of them on the New York, Mahoning and Western railroad. American workingmen held secret meetings, and hundreds of notices headed by a skull and cross-bones were scattered about the city. Signed "MANY CITIZENS," the circular warned the village council and contractors that Italian labor "must and shall be prohibited from working on the public works of this city." A brief in the Portland Daily Press added that "the bad feeling may soon result in mob violence."

According to the most widely printed Cleveland dispatch, 200 Italian laborers struck for higher wages on August 1 and were discharged. When they demanded their pay they were so "boisterous" that the paymaster hesitated to hand over the money. The strikers then procured a rope and were "just about to hang him" when the sheriff appeared with a posse and rescued him.

A second account, credited to a special from Findlay, said the trouble began over "some trivial matters" and that the paymaster arrived with the money only to be besieged by Italians, each demanding to be paid first and disputing the amount. In this version the posse "dispersed the rioters for the time being," and American laborers, whose feeling was "very bitter," threatened "to clean them all out before morning."

No report of arrests or charges against the strikers appears in the coverage. A later brief said that about 250 Italians quit work on the Mahoning grade near Findlay on August 6 and that Americans immediately took their places. Many of the Italians were left destitute and, according to the same brief, "threatened vengeance on the contractors."

All the reports found ran in white newspapers, and none came from a Findlay paper. On August 2 the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer ran the shorter wire as "Italians on the Rampage," ending with "great excitement and fears of another outbreak," and the Washington Critic printed the same text among its news briefs. The Maysville Evening Bulletin ran it a day later as "Italians Strike."

The Findlay special appeared the same day in the St. Paul Daily Globe as "A Race Riot," in a Michigan Telegram-Herald as "A Riot Threatened," and in the Beatrice Daily Express as "Riotous Italians." A week later two Kansas papers reprinted it under "Italians Must Go," with a subhead announcing that American laborers threatened to "Clean Them Out in Ohio." Both versions cast the Italians as the aggressors, and none of the papers commented on the threat against them.

The paymaster's name varied from paper to paper: "Hygenro" in Wheeling, "Henry Jarero" in Washington and "Hy Jenero" in Maysville, all in the same wire text, while the Findlay special called him "Henry Jones." The accounts also differed on the cause, one naming a strike for higher wages and the other a disagreement over "trivial matters."

reader.title: Findlay Italian strikers' attempted hanging of a paymaster
bases: Italian railroad laborers who had struck over wages and pay threatened to hang the paymaster during the dispute, and a sheriff's posse intervened (A4, A6, A8).

No one was killed: the strikers were stopped by a sheriff's posse before they could hang the paymaster (A4, A6), and the threat arose from a wage and pay dispute, not under a pretext of justice, race or tradition (A4, A8).

Two differently worded Cleveland dispatches, one of them credited to a Findlay special, agree that about 200 striking Italians demanded their pay, procured a rope to hang the paymaster and were stopped by a sheriff's posse (A4, A6, A8), though they disagree on the paymaster's name.

accounts.label: Cleveland wire ('Italians on the Rampage' version)
accounts.gist: 200 Italians struck for higher wages and were discharged; when they demanded their pay they were so 'boisterous' that the paymaster hesitated, so they procured a rope and were about to hang him when the sheriff and a posse rescued him.

accounts.label: Findlay special via Cleveland ('A Race Riot' version)
accounts.gist: Trouble over 'trivial matters' led 200 Italians to strike and besiege paymaster Henry Jones over who was paid first and how much; they got a rope to hang him, a posse dispersed them, and American laborers threatened to drive the Italians out.

framing.detail: The shorter wire, headed 'Italians on the Rampage' or 'Italians Strike', presented the strikers as the aggressors and noted 'fears of another outbreak'.

The Findlay-special version, headed 'A Race Riot', 'A Riot Threatened' or 'Riotous Italians', cast it as Italian against American laborers and reported without comment the Americans' threat to 'clean them all out'.
Kansas weeklies reran the Findlay special a week later under 'Italians Must Go', with the subhead 'American Laborers Threaten to Clean Them Out in Ohio'.

conflicts.note: The first three are spellings in the same wire text; 'Henry Jones' comes from the separately worded Findlay special. No local Findlay paper was found to settle it.
